title: An expression as a graph
objectives: Draw an expression as a graph of operations and compute its forward values.

screens.title: Which input matters most?
screens.prose: A model computes $L = (ab + c)f$ from four inputs. Today $a = 1.5$, $b = -2$, $c = 4$ and $f = -3$, so $L = -3$. Move one slider at a time by one step of 0.5, then put it back.
screens.question: Which input moves $L$ the most for a move of 0.5?

options.why: A step in $b$ moves $L$ by 2.25. A step in $a$ moves it by 3.
A step in $c$ moves $L$ by 1.5, half as much as a step in $a$.
A step in $f$ moves $L$ by only 0.5, because $f$ multiplies $ab + c = 1$.

hints.text: Put each slider back to its start before you move the next one.
Read the number under $L$ after each move.
A step in $a$ takes $L$ from $-3$ to 0; in $b$ to $-5.25$; in $c$ to $-4.5$; in $f$ to $-2.5$.

feedback.correct: A step of 0.5 in $a$ moves $L$ by 3, more than any other input. This course finds those rates without moving every slider.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare how far $L$ moves for each one-step move.

explain.text: From $L = -3$, a step in $a$ gives 0, in $b$ gives $-5.25$, in $c$ gives $-4.5$ and in $f$ gives $-2.5$. The biggest move, 3, comes from $a$. The rest of this level explains why.

screens.title: Draw the graph
screens.prose: You worked $L$ out in three steps. Drawn as a **computation graph**, each box is one operation and the leaves $a$, $b$, $c$, $f$ are its inputs. Each arrow carries a value forward into the next box.
screens.question: Drag each value into the box it feeds.

hints.text: Each box names its own inputs on its label.
The box $d = e + c$ adds two things: the first product and $c$.
$a$ and $b$ feed $e$; $e$ and $c$ feed $d$; $d$ and $f$ feed $L$.

feedback.correct: Six arrows: $a, b \to e$, then $e, c \to d$, then $d, f \to L$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read each box: its label names the two values it takes in.

byKey.c: You fed $c$ into the first product. In $(ab + c)f$, $c$ is added after $ab$ is formed.
byKey.f: You put $f$ in early. It multiplies the whole bracket, so it meets $d$ in the last box.
byKey.e: You fed $e$ into the last box. The bracket $ab + c$ needs $e$ first.

explain.text: Each box takes the values on its incoming arrows. $a$ and $b$ make $e$, $e$ and $c$ make $d$, and $d$ and $f$ make $L$.

screens.title: The forward pass
screens.prose: Push the numbers forward one box at a time. A box can be worked out once every arrow into it carries a value.
screens.question: Fill in the value each box computes.

hints.text: Start with the box whose inputs are all leaves.

feedback.correct: $e = -3$, $d = 1$, $L = -3$: the value you saw under $L$ on the first screen.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work left to right, one box at a time.

byKey.carried-sign: You carried $e = 3$ into the sum. With $e = -3$, $d = -3 + 4 = 1$.
byKey.used-e: You multiplied $e$ by $f$. The last box multiplies $d$ by $f$: $1 \times (-3)$.

explain.text: Each box waits for its inputs: $e = 1.5 \times (-2) = -3$, then $d = -3 + 4 = 1$, then $L = 1 \times (-3) = -3$. This left-to-right sweep is the **forward pass**.

screens.title: A power and an exponential
screens.prose: A second expression, $M = e^{xy} + z^2$, at $x = 0.5$, $y = 2$, $z = -1.5$. The graph gives the exponential and the square a box each.
screens.question: Run the forward pass. What is $M$, to 3 decimal places?

hints.text: Work out $p$, then $q$, then $s$, then add.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work one box at a time, left to right.

byKey.neg-square: You took $s = -2.25$. A square is never negative: $(-1.5)^2 = 2.25$.

screens.title: One box too few
screens.prose: Sam draws $(ab + c)f$ with two boxes: $d = ab + c$, then $L = df$. Sam says fewer boxes means less work later.
screens.question: What goes wrong with Sam's graph?

options.text: The box $d = ab + c$ holds two operations, so its derivative needs the chain rule inside it again
Nothing: two boxes give the same value of $L$ with less drawing and less work later
options.why: You checked the forward value, which agrees. The trouble comes later, when each box must give a simple derivative.

options.text: It gives a different value of $L$ from the three-box graph
options.why: You expected the value to change. Sam still gets $d = 1$ and $L = -3$.

options.text: It adds $c$ before it multiplies $a$ by $b$, so the order is wrong
options.why: You read the box as $a(b + c)$. Sam's box still forms $ab$ first, then adds $c$.

hints.text: The forward value is the same. Think about what each box will be asked for next.
Each box will need a derivative for each input.
A box with one operation has a one-line derivative. Sam's box hides a product and a sum.

feedback.correct: Right. The values agree, but one box with two operations hides a product inside a sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare what each box does, not the final value.

byKey.fine: You checked the forward value, which agrees. The trouble is that Sam's box hides a product inside a sum.

explain.text: Sam's graph gives $L = -3$ too. But the box $d = ab + c$ is a product and a sum, so working with it means the chain rule again. One operation per box keeps every step to one simple rule.

screens.title: A value used twice
screens.prose: Now $K = ab + a$, with $a = 1.5$ and $b = -2$. The value $a$ is used twice. In a graph we draw $a$ once, with an arrow to every box that uses it.
screens.question: How many arrows leave the leaf $a$?

hints.text: Count the boxes that use $a$.
$a$ goes into the product and into the sum.
Two boxes use $a$, so two arrows leave it.

feedback.correct: Two arrows leave $a$: one into $e = ab$, one into $K = e + a$. Level 2 shows what this does to gradients.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the boxes that take $a$ in.

byKey.one: You drew one arrow, as if $a$ were used once. It feeds the product and the sum.

explain.text: $a$ is one value, so it is one node. It feeds 2 boxes, so 2 arrows leave it, and $K = -3 + 1.5 = -1.5$.

screens.title: The forward pass in code
screens.prose: Each box of the graph becomes one line of Python. Write `forward_pass(a, b, c, f)` for $L = (ab + c)f$. Return a dict of the three box values, keyed `"e"`, `"d"` and `"L"`.
screens.question: Write `forward_pass(a, b, c, f)`.

widget.how: Submit runs 5 hidden tests: the course inputs and four others. Each dict must equal the expected one exactly.

hints.text: Write one line per box, in the order the forward pass meets them.
The first line is `e = a * b`.
`e = a * b`, then `d = e + c`, then `L = d * f`, then return the dict.

feedback.correct: Three lines, one per box, in the order of the forward pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare your dict with the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the course inputs. It expects `{'e': -3.0, 'd': 1.0, 'L': -3.0}`.

explain.text: Each box is one assignment, and the order of the lines is the order of the forward pass. The dict keeps every intermediate value, which the backward pass will need.

screens.title: What a graph records
screens.prose: A computation graph has one box per operation. Its leaves are the inputs, and its arrows carry values forward. The forward pass computes each box once all its inputs are known: $$e = ab, \quad d = e + c, \quad L = df.$$
screens.question: When can the forward pass compute a box?

options.text: As soon as every arrow into it carries a value
Only when it is the leftmost box not yet done
options.why: You read the drawing's layout as the rule. A box's place on the page does not matter; its inputs do.

options.text: Only after the output $L$ is known
options.why: You ran it backwards. $L$ is computed last, from the boxes before it.

options.text: Only once every leaf in the whole graph is used
options.why: You waited for the whole graph. A box needs only its own inputs.

hints.text: What did you need before you could compute $d$?
$d$ needs $e$ and $c$, nothing else.
A box is ready once its own inputs have values.

feedback.correct: A box is ready once its own inputs are known.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what $d$ needed.

explain.text: $d = e + c$ needed only $e$ and $c$. So any box can be computed once its own inputs have values, and the output comes last.

screens.title: A P&L as a graph
screens.prose: A £500,000 book holds 60% in a share bought at £200 and 40% in one bought at £50. Today they close at $p_1 = 206$ and $p_2 = 49$. The P&L runs prices to returns, returns to a weighted sum, and that sum to pounds.
screens.question: Run the forward pass. What is the P&L, in pounds?

hints.text: Start with the two returns.

feedback.correct: The returns are 0.03 and $-0.02$, so $R = 0.01$ and the P&L is £5,000.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work box by box: returns, then $R$, then pounds.

byKey.return-only: You stopped at $R = 0.01$. The last box turns it into pounds: £5,000.
byKey.sign: You dropped the minus sign on $r_2$. The second share fell from £50 to £49.

ideas: A computation graph has one box per operation, the inputs as leaves, and arrows that carry values forward.
The forward pass computes each box once its own inputs are known; the output comes last.
A value used twice is one node with two arrows leaving it.

formula.name: The course expression
formula.tex: e = ab, \quad d = e + c, \quad L = df

summary.trap: A box that holds two operations hides a chain rule inside it. Give every operation its own box.

quiz.prose: Draw $y = (x - w)^2 + 3x$ as a computation graph, with one box per operation.
quiz.question: How many boxes does it have?

feedback.correct: Four boxes: $x - w$, its square, $3x$, and the sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite. List each operation once.

byKey.merged: You put $(x - w)^2$ in one box. The difference and the square are two operations.

explain.text: The operations are $s = x - w$, $t = s^2$, $u = 3x$ and $y = t + u$: 4 boxes. The 3 and $x$ are inputs, not boxes.

quiz.prose: A graph computes $s = p + q$, then $g = sr$, at $p = 2$, $q = -5$, $r = 4$.
quiz.question: What value does the forward pass give for $g$?

byKey.no-sum: You multiplied $p$ by $r$. The product takes the sum $s$.

explain.text: The forward pass computes $s = 2 + (-5) = -3$ first. Then $g = sr = -3 \times 4 = -12$.

quiz.prose: In a computation graph the arrows point from inputs towards the output.
quiz.question: In the forward pass, what does each arrow carry?

options.text: The value of the box it leaves
A derivative of the box it enters
options.why: You jumped ahead to the backward pass. Forward, an arrow carries a value.
You sent the output everywhere. Each arrow carries its own box's value.
You read the label as the message. The arrow carries a number.

feedback.correct: Each arrow carries the value of the box it leaves.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about $e \to d$ in the course graph.

explain.text: In the course graph the arrow $e \to d$ carries $e = -3$ into the sum. Every arrow carries a value forward like that.
